Lose the Superbird: The Road Runner Hemi RTS Show Car Is the Wildest Winged Mopar of 1970
87 photos
Photo: Mecum
What's the most famous Mopar three-letter acronym of them all? GTX? GTS? TRX? AAR? SRT? ACR? R/T? HEMI? The last two aren't three letters by themselves, but their average is right on the money. But how about RTS? I’ll give you a moment to remember that body style, the platform, and powertrains. No, it’s a trick hint, there was no Chrysler Motors Corporation automobile named “RTS.” There were five of them, all Plymouths, all from 1970.
Standing for Rapid Transit System, it was Plymouth's loud, tire-roasting 1970 marketing blitz, cooked up specifically to match Dodge's beloved Scat Pack of 1968 and turn respectable family showrooms into high-octane sanctuaries for horsepower-obsessed youth.
Far from being just a catchy slogan slapped onto glossy brochures, the Rapid Transit System was an entire performance ecosystem. Plymouth urged dealers to build dedicated Rapid Transit System Centers stocked with High Impact colors, beefy drivetrains, aggressive axle gears, and race-bred parts forged in NASCAR, Trans-Am, and NHRA battles. Its purpose was bluntly simple: convince restless kids that Plymouth wasn't just grandma's Valiant store, and move serious iron fast.
The campaign ran through the 1970 and 1971 model years, landing at the glorious peak of Detroit's horsepower mania right before insurance actuaries dropped an anvil on the party. Five street-bruising production models anchored the official RTS lineup: the Road Runner, GTX, 'Cuda, Duster 340, and full-size Sport Fury GT, while the winged 1970 Road Runner Superbird loomed nearby like a hyperactive cartoon bird that accidentally swallowed an Acme rocket.
Photo: Mecum Truth be told, the Superbird was the only production vehicle that was styled just right for the Rapid Transit System , although that was a pure coincidence. Ma’ Mopar never intended to use the ‘Bird as a sales honeycomb for buyers. However, the preposterously in-your-face looks of the NASCAR-homologation muscle car served that purpose in full, planted in showrooms to catch the eye of passers-by, and lure them in the webs of a shrewd salesman that would convince them into a new car.
Because regular showroom muscle cars apparently looked too polite for 1970, Plymouth also launched the Rapid Transit System Caravan, a traveling road show hauled to dealerships, racetracks, and auto shows nationwide. Former Hot Wheels designer Harry Bradley sketched wild custom interpretations of Plymouth's lineup, birthing four one-off showstoppers across 1970 and 1971: a 1970 'Cuda 440, a 1970 Duster 340, a restyled 1971 Road Runner, and the magnificent headliner standing before us.
Meet the one-of-a-kind 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner built specifically for the Rapid Transit System Caravan. While fabricator Byron Grenfell massaged the Duster and Chuck Miller's Styline Customs built the 'Cuda and later 1971 Road Runner, Plymouth entrusted this B-body bruiser to Roman's Chariot Shop in Cleveland, Ohio.
Photo: Mecum Showing just 1,700 miles on the odometer today, it spent far more time snapping necks under spotlights than dodging potholes on American highways, or slaying rivals at stoplights. After all, its looks alone could subdue any potential contender into second thoughts.
Subtlety took a sabbatical sick day hike and went AWOL when this coupe rolled into the paint booth. Roman's Chariot Shop drenched the body in candy gold beneath a pearl white roof, contrasting the glare with a flat black hood and flat black decklid. Lest anyone mistake it for a quiet commuter, oversized Road Runner birds were painted straight into the bodywork, practically daring Wile E. Coyote to drop an crate of dynamite at his own paws.
The custom bodywork went far beyond loud paint, as the shop reworked the sheet metal like kids handed unlimited clay and a welding torch. Enlarged air scoops give the flanks a hungry, “inhale-the-zip-code” attitude, while a molded rear spoiler finishes the tail.
Photo: Mecum (Sidenote: I don’t know who copied who on that rear deck lid element: Plymouth from Chrysler, or vice-versa? The Chrysler 300 Hurst from that same year had a strikingly similar wing, but far more subtle and discrete. The Road Runner RTS was about as low-profile as a one-bore punt gun blast at a puritans’ wedding ceremony).
The rear wheel wells were enlarged and flared out 4 inches over Ansen Sprint wheels, and shaved door handles leave the sides smoother than a used-car salesman's alibi. Up front, Plymouth's factory face entered the witness protection program. In its place sits a plastic honeycomb grille flanked by 9-inch square Cibie headlights, giving the Road Runner an intense glare that made stock 1970 B-bodies look half asleep.
Walk around back and a custom one-piece tail lens stretches cleanly across the tail panel, handing anyone left behind at a stoplight a full-width crimson receipt for their bruised ego.
Photo: Mecum Best of all, this wasn't some hollow fiberglass parade float pushed onto a turntable by nervous teen interns. Lift that flat black hood and you're staring straight at Chrysler's mythic 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8, factory-rated at a famously introvert 425 hp. Paired with a bulletproof TorqueFlite automatic transmission and a stump-pulling 4.10 rear axle, this elephant-powered Plymouth had the mechanical violence to back up every loud inch of its wild custom suit .
Pop those shaved doors and the cabin stays refreshingly focused while the exterior throws a disco party. Bucket seats straddle a center console, giving the driver a proper perch for wrangling 490 lb-ft of crank twist without sliding into the passenger's lap. Provenance hounds get spoiled silly here, too, with an official letter from the Chrysler-Plymouth News Bureau and the original, one-of-a-kind Rapid Transit floor runners crafted for both sides of the vehicle.
Surviving the 1970s intact as a factory show car was roughly as easy as smuggling a rhino in rut past TSA, and this gold Hemi vanished once its tour ended. For 20 years, Mopar fans feared the crusher had won. Then, in 1991, noted sleuths Steve Juliano and Ed Meyer tracked the missing bird down in Kalamazoo, Michigan, rescuing Plymouth's wildest rolling billboard before rust or bad taste could finish the job.
Photo: Mecum Even with a featherweight 1,700 miles showing, decades out of the spotlight meant the custom bruiser needed expert revival. In 2000, Ken Heckett restored the Road Runner to period-perfect glory, honoring every flare, scoop, and painted wing.
With its 1970 Caravan 'Cuda sibling having hammered for $2.2 million in 2023, the four surviving Rapid Transit System show cars now occupy Mopar's penthouse suite alongside the rarest winged warriors Plymouth ever built.
In 2019, at the Mecum Indy event, the 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner Rapid Transit hammered 310,000 legal money of the United States of Automobile ($341k with the mandatory buyer’s fees). Before that, in November of 2018, it made a star appearance at the MCACN show – see the video embedded below, courtesy of Lou Costabile, the vlogger who’s always one snapshot away from musle car royalty .
Photo: Mecum It currently stands as the second-most expensive Road Runner ever (excluding the Superbirds and Richard Petty’s 1971 championship-winning car). Now, after decades turning heads in elite collections, this unmistakable slice of factory-sanctioned 1970 madness is strutting back under the auction spotlights.
Complete with its 426 Hemi thunder , Roman's Chariot Shop metalwork, News Bureau letter, and original dual floor runners, the one-off 1970 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner Rapid Transit System Caravan show car is offered for sale at the Mecum Kissimmee 2027 auction. Care to make a guess (educated of enthusiastic) on the high bid?
